text: The SS Columbia (1880–1907) was a cargo and passenger steamship owned initially by the Oregon Railway and Navigation Company and later by the San Francisco and Portland Steamship Company. Constructed in 1880 by the John Roach & Sons shipyard in Chester, Pennsylvania, as Hull No. 193 for the Oregon Steamship Company, which was acquired by the Oregon Railway and Navigation Company in 1879, construction began in September 1879 and the ship was launched on February 24, 1880 at 11:40 a.m. Both the Bureau Veritas and American Shipmasters' Association oversaw its building. Despite Roach’s initial refusal to install incandescent light bulbs due to fire concerns, the ship became the first to carry a dynamo powering electric lights instead of oil lamps and the first commercial use of electric light bulbs outside of Thomas Edison's Menlo Park, New Jersey laboratory. After attending Edison’s New Year's Eve demonstration, Henry Villard, president of the Oregon Railway and Navigation Company, ordered the installation of an Edison Lighting System, making Columbia the first commercial vessel to use the incandescent bulb and Edison’s first commercial order for the light bulb. The lighting system was installed in May 1880, with the first lighting occurring on May 2, 1880, and the bulbs carried aboard by Francis R. Upton. The system was successful, with chief engineers reporting no failures after 415 hours and 45 minutes of continuous use. The ship completed sea trials, sailed around Cape Horn to San Francisco with 13 locomotives, 200 railroad cars, and supplies, made a stop in Rio de Janeiro where Emperor Pedro II of Brazil viewed the electric lights, and used light bulbs attached to a tallow-covered cable to inspect the propeller shaft and rudder while passing through the Straits of Magellan. Upon arrival in San Francisco, the original carbon filament bulbs were replaced with newer bamboo filament bulbs sent by Edison. The ship safely arrived in Portland on August 24, 1880, though insurance companies were initially reluctant to underwrite it. Columbia operated a regular service between Portland and San Francisco and, after the Alaskan was sunk in 1889, carried its captain and crew to Astoria. The success of the Edison lighting system led to adoption by other shipping companies, including the British Cunard Line, with the SS Servia becoming the first major ocean liner lit by incandescent bulbs in 1881. The Columbia was highly reliable, with a record of being on the route for less than one night in fifteen years. In July 1895, the original Edison generators were removed and replaced with modern ones, and the dynamos were later donated to the Smithsonian Institution and The Henry Ford in Dearborn, Michigan. The Oregon Railway and Navigation Company was taken over by the Union Pacific Railroad in 1904, and the Columbia and the George W. Elder were transferred to the new subsidiary, the San Francisco and Portland Steamship Company. In 1905, the George W. Elder struck a rock and sank, later being refloated and purchased by the North Pacific Steamship Company, and the Columbia collided with a wood barge in the Columbia River, resulting in damage requiring repair in San Francisco. On February 1, 1906, the Columbia collided with a log raft in dense fog, with no damage to the ship, though the captain anchored until the fog lifted. On January 30, 1898, the Columbia broke the speed record between San Francisco and Portland, traveling in just under two days with a delay of one hour due to stops, shaving one hour off the previous record. On October 3, 1900, the Columbia collided with the ferryboat Berkeley in San Francisco due to misinterpreted signals, damaging the bow of the Columbia and destroying one of the Berkeley’s lifeboats, leading both ships to be taken out of service. The George W. Elder temporarily replaced the Columbia on its route. On September 14, 1902, the Columbia ran aground near Astoria due to low tide and was refloated at high tide and returned to Portland the following night. During a refit at the Union Iron Works in 1906, the ship was damaged by the San Francisco earthquake, knocking off its supports, rolling to starboard, and hitting the dock, with its iron hull damaging the hydraulic drydock. The ship was sent to Hunter’s Point for permanent repairs, during which the crew abandoned ship after a steam pipe explosion. The Columbia was temporarily replaced by the steamer Costa Rica and the Barracouta. It returned to service on January 17, 1907, and was trapped in an ice pack near St. Helens, Oregon for four days, with the Aragonia successfully breaking through the ice to free it. After returning to San Francisco, the ship appeared unscathed. Designed by Edward Faron, the Columbia was 300 feet (91 m) long with 310 feet (94 m) above water, had a beam of 38 feet 6 inches (11.73 m), a depth of 23 feet (7.0 m), and was powered by two compound condensing steam engines with 42.5-inch and 82-inch by 54-inch strokes driving a single Hirsch four-bladed propeller of 16 feet (4.9 m) diameter and 27 feet (8.2 m) mean pitch, operating at 65 revolutions per minute. The propeller could be removed individually or all at once. The ship had six boilers, each 12 feet (3.7 m) in diameter and 12 feet 6 inches (3.81 m) long, operating at 80 pounds per square inch (550 kPa) pressure. It carried a maximum of 300 tons of coal, had an estimated top speed of 16 knots (30 km/h; 18 mph), and included a single donkey boiler and an auxiliary steam engine for bilge and water supply, plus a second auxiliary engine for electricity. It had a Brigantine rig with over 15,000 yards (14,000 m) of canvas on two iron masts. The ship had four decks—Spar, Main, Hurricane, and a fourth—each with iron framing and four watertight compartments. It featured electric fire alarms, annunciators, hydrants, electric head and side lights powered by an auxiliary dynamo, and telegraph communication between the bridge and engine room. The cargo holds had double steam-powered elevators. Passenger amenities were highly innovative and luxurious, including a large refrigeration room in the stern capable of maintaining a constant cold temperature, ventilation and heating systems, a Bohemian glass shade illuminated by an electric bulb in the main saloon, frosted glass fixtures for other bulbs, French walnut, Hungarian ash, mahogany, and maple paneling in the dining room, wooden furniture and carpeting, telephones in key rooms, and electrical indicators and monitoring equipment on the bridge. First-class staterooms accommodated 250 individuals and steerage 600 passengers, with paneling and furniture similar to first-class Pullman rail cars, including folding berths. Fresh-water plumbing was included. All 120 light bulbs were connected via separate circuits to four 6-kilowatt Edison A Type "long legged Mary-Ann" dynamos, with the fourth boosting the magnetic fields of the others at a lower voltage, each capable of powering 60 bulbs. Voltage adjustments were made by observing bulb brightness in the engine room. Wiring used molten paraffin and cotton in rubber tube casings, with wires painted to distinguish positive and negative charges. The electrical system mirrored Menlo Park designs, with oil lamps available as backup. On July 20, 1907, Columbia departed San Francisco with 251 passengers and crew for Portland under Captain Peter Doran. As evening approached, the ship became shrouded in fog about 12 miles (19 km) off Shelter Cove, and Doran refused to slow down despite the whistle of the lumber schooner San Pedro being heard nearby. Neither vessel reduced speed, and the rolling waves caused many passengers to go to their cabins due to seasickness. Fifteen minutes later, San Pedro approached directly. Doran ordered full reverse, but it was too late. At 12:22 a.m. on July 21, 1907, San Pedro struck the starboard side of Columbia, damaging the bow of the wooden-hulled San Pedro and holed the Columbia, causing it to list to starboard and sink by the bow. Passenger William L. Smith described the impact as "soft," while Otilla Liedelt reported it as severe. Doran ordered lifeboats to be launched, with Smith going from cabin to cabin to ensure passenger safety. Many passengers were seasick and did not respond, while others prepared to abandon ship. Smith observed a family holding hands in their cabin. As the ship sank, Liedelt noted that Doran tied the whistle cord down on the bridge and remained there, waving his hands in a final salute. After the bridge submerged, the whistle stopped. The ship developed a noticeable list to starboard, allowing Lifeboat Number Four to be launched without lowering. Eight and a half minutes after the collision, the ship began its final plunge, with the stern rising and the bow entering the water in seconds. A large explosion occurred, dragging many people back to the surface. While survivors believed the explosion was from a boiler, Chief Engineer Jackson stated it did not explode, as he stood directly above them when the ship pitched. Another theory is that a massive release of trapped air caused the explosion. Among those in the water was 16-year-old Maybelle Watson from Berkeley, who, after being thrown from a capsizing lifeboat, found a young schoolteacher flailing due to a lifebelt fastened backwards. Maybelle helped her stand upright and keep her head above water until rescued by Officer Hawse’s lifeboat. A total of 88 passengers and crew, including all children on board, perished in the sinking. Due to the rapid sinking, many lifeboats could not be launched. After the sinking, the lifeboats of Columbia and San Pedro launched a rescue effort assisted by the steamers Roanoke and George W. Elder. The San Pedro, carrying 390,000 ft (118,872 m) of redwood, remained afloat and rescued nearly 80 survivors, many of whom were forced to hold on to each other to avoid being carried away by lapping waves.

During the sinking of the Columbia, 88 passengers and crew, including all children on board, lost their lives due to the rapid descent of the ship. Many lifeboats could not be launched because of the speed of the sinking. After the disaster, the lifeboats from the Columbia and San Pedro launched a rescue operation, assisted by the steamers Roanoke and George W. Elder, the latter being one of Columbia’s previous running mates. Although severely damaged and partially sunk with a noticeable list, the San Pedro’s hull, carrying 390,000 ft (118,872 m) of redwood, remained afloat. Nearly 80 survivors were brought aboard the San Pedro, many of whom had to hold onto each other to avoid being swept away by lapping waves on the semi-submerged deck. The George W. Elder also towed the damaged San Pedro to shore. Hull inspector John K. Bulger, who had inspected the Columbia eight months earlier with O.F. Bolles—coincidentally the ship’s first captain—testified that the vessel had four watertight bulkheads, meeting modern safety standards requiring only three. However, Bulger admitted that if one compartment was punctured, water would cascade over the bulkheads, causing the ship to sink, a scenario similar to the RMS Titanic’s sinking in 1912. He later retestified that two flooded compartments would lead to disaster, not one. Despite this, the bulkheads likely provided little delay in water ingress. The San Francisco Examiner reported that the Columbia, an iron-hulled vessel, suffered a major impact, with its brittle, aged iron plates cracking and a seven-foot gash at the forward hatch allowing unimpeded water entry. Captain Doran of the Columbia and First Officer Hendrickson of the San Pedro were found most responsible for the collision; Hendrickson’s license was revoked for five years, and Captain Magnus Hanson of the San Pedro was found to have given insufficient orders and failed to reach the bridge when warned of fog, resulting in a one-year license revocation. Despite these errors, survivors and the press commended most crew members for their bravery and lifesaving actions. Third Officer Hawse of the Columbia, however, received little praise; he was reported to have shown aggressive and indifferent behavior, threatening to throw survivors overboard and claiming he would have shot them if he had a .45. He blamed Captain Hanson for denying survivors boarding his vessel, which he claimed caused many deaths. Survivors denied Hawse’s account of Hanson’s actions, and rumors spread about Hawse having a morphine addiction; Doctor S.B. Foster at the U.S. Marine Hospital noted Hawse had requested the drug three times. Hawse was arrested on July 29, 1907, while living in Second Officer Richard Agerup’s home in San Francisco, showing signs of paranoia during arrest and was admitted to the Central Emergency Hospital’s detention ward. After the sinking, the San Francisco and Portland Steamship Company leased the City of Panama to replace the Columbia. On August 8, 1907, the City of Panama collided with the grounded steam schooner Alliance near the Willamette and Columbia Rivers; due to the Alliance’s wooden hull, the City of Panama sustained only minor damage. Richard Agerup, the City of Panama’s second officer, had been on the Columbia’s bridge the night it sank. The Columbia’s sinking, along with earlier losses of the Valencia, Clallam, and City of Rio de Janeiro, eroded public confidence in shipping lines and inspectors. Despite the tragedy, key lessons were not learned. On August 29, 1929, over 22 years later, the passenger steamer San Juan collided with the oil tanker S.C.T. Dodd in dense fog, sinking in just three minutes and killing 77 people. The San Juan’s sinking closely mirrored that of the Columbia, sharing similar design, shipyard, route, and being outdated iron-hulled steamers. The San Pedro was repaired and continued serving along the California coast until being sold to foreign owners in 1920, after which it sank that same year. The Punta Gorda Light was established in response to the disaster, and rusting debris from the Columbia—including a boiler and bulkhead—remains visible near the northern section of the Lost Coast Hiking Trail. Between 1899 and 1907, at least eight other ships sank in the area, including the St. Paul, whose rusted boilers are still visible in the surf at Punta Gorda. The coordinates of the incident are 39°57′29.43″N 124°11′2.26″W (39.9581750°N 124.1839611°W).
